prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction and experimental discovery of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators

statement.case_for: Having read all eight opening ballots, I have moved my preferred configuration from B015 to B006. My own first choice, tunnel magnetoresistance, was ranked by nobody else, and I should not treat my familiarity with the spintronics literature as evidence that the committee can reach certainty on it. B006 is the candidate with the broadest support (seven of eight ballots, four in the top three), and it passes the tests I care about most. The key claims were verified by direct measurement. Molenkamp's group observed the quantized edge conductance of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells in 2007, and Hasan's ARPES work showed the three-dimensional phase in Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3. Kane supplies the theoretical proposal of the Z2 invariant that gave the field its structure. The experiments are original, not a later and more elegant version of something done earlier. More than fifteen years of independent confirmation across transport, ARPES and many material families make the result stable. The impact reaches from our understanding of band theory to materials discovery. A three-person prize covering theory, the two-dimensional experiment and the three-dimensional experiment is a fair reflection of who did the original work, with the caveat noted below.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Kane and Mele wrote the 2005 papers together, and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal for HgTe is what made Molenkamp's experiment possible, yet Zhang has died and cannot be credited. A three-name limit forces us to leave out Mele, who is arguably inseparable from Kane, and the supplied credit omits others who made early contributions to the 3D case (Moore, Balents, Fu). I would not want the committee to settle on a trio just because the ballots happen to converge on it. There is also a novelty question because the 2016 prize already recognised topological phases of matter. I think that is answerable, since 2016 concerned topological phase transitions and quantum Hall-type invariants in model systems, whereas this is time-reversal-invariant topology in real materials, but it must be argued explicitly. If the committee decides the credit cannot be assigned with confidence, B017 is my next choice, not a forced B006.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B006 first because the Kane-Mele model is a clean, sharp prediction followed by a decisive transport experiment, with a large conceptual reach through bulk-boundary correspondence, and because the timing is ripe. He also recognises that only three names fit and that Mele is a close partner of Kane.
responses.response: I agree with the timing and with the experimental confirmation. I would put more weight than Bernhard on the experiments, which is why I support Molenkamp and Hasan alongside Kane. But I do not think the Mele problem can be set aside as a regrettable detail. If we credit Kane without Mele we are making a statement about who originated the Z2 insulator, and the 2005 papers do not clearly support separating them. I would ask the committee to look at what each of the 2005 papers actually contributed, and at whether Mele has an independent claim to the first 2005 proposal, before we settle on the trio. My support depends on that check.

responses.point: Eriksson puts magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first because the quantitative magic-angle prediction was followed by experimental confirmation, the theory-experiment loop that he values. He calls the single-particle picture stable but notes that the pairing mechanism is still debated, and that junior authors did much of the key work.
responses.response: I ranked B017 second myself and I share the admiration for the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction and the 2018 devices. But I come out at a different place on maturity. The correlated phases and the origin of the superconductivity are not understood, and the field is about eight years old. We would be crediting an observation whose interpretation is still in motion. I also have a procedural worry that the credited experimental person is the group leader while Cao and Fatemi did the measurements, and the Nobel statutes allow no more than three. For me that makes B017 a strong candidate for a few years from now, and B006 the better choice today. I am happy to be persuaded otherwise if Olle can show that the correlated insulator and superconductivity results are already settled by several independent groups.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first because they extend what can be measured, with 1e-18 uncertainties, reproduced in many laboratories and pointing toward a redefinition of the second. He sees the two-person Katori-Ye configuration as clean.
responses.response: I agree that this is a well-verified instrument advance and I like the clean two-name attribution. It is the candidate that comes closest to the tools-that-open-doors criterion that I find persuasive. My reservation is the one that Stefan himself mentions, that Hall and Hansch (2005) and Wineland (2012) already honoured the underlying toolbox. The discovery content so far is upper limits and precision, not a new phenomenon. I would like to hear whether the committee thinks the redefinition of the second, which has not happened yet, is a precondition for the prize. If it is, B047 may be a better choice in a later year. If it is not, B047 stays a serious contender and I would rank it above B038 or B022.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the platform on which superconducting quantum processors rest, strongly reproduced and timely, and a natural follow-on to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits.
responses.response: Goran knows this field far better than I do, and I accept that the experimental demonstration by Wallraff and Schoelkopf and the Blais proposal are original and widely confirmed. My difficulty is the one that several of us have noted, that the 2025 prize covered the circuit foundations, and Girvin and Huang, who were co-authors of the 2004 proposal, are missing from the credit. A second superconducting-circuit prize within a year of the first would need a very clear statement of what is distinct. I ranked B038 seventh, and I would raise it only if the committee can answer the 2025 overlap and the credit gap convincingly.

uncertainties: Whether Mele can be separated from Kane on the 2005 papers, and whether a three-name limit makes a B006 prize fair without him.
Whether the 2016 topological-phases prize leaves enough room for a second topological prize, and how the citation should be worded to make the distinction.
Whether the B015 history (Julliere 1975, Miyazaki and Moodera 1995, Parkin and Yuasa MgO 2004) can be given a defensible three-name attribution; I could not make that case from the shortlist alone.
Whether the magic-angle superconducting and correlated phases will be settled enough in the near term to move B017 above B006.
statement.conflict_note: No personal conflict that requires recusal is apparent from my profile for the preferred B006 configuration. I note for transparency that Katori (B047) is at the University of Tokyo, where I am a Fellow since 2025, and Miyazaki (B015) is at Tohoku University, where I lectured in 2026 and where I have longstanding exchanges with the microscopy community. Those are institutional contacts and not collaborations, and I have no joint publications with the credited names that I know of. Goran Johansson, who champions B038, is a Chalmers physics colleague of mine, which is worth recording but does not bear on my ranking.
